title: Why and When to Fine-Tune
source_excerpt:
1. Why and When to Fine-Tune

What you will learn: Fine-tuning modifies the internal weights of a pre-trained language model using domain-specific dataset pairs. While prompt engineering guides the model via context and RAG provides external knowledge, fine-tuning permanently adapts behavioral form, complex formatting adherence, tone, and specialized shorthand syntax.

title: Prompting vs Fine-Tuning vs RAG
source_excerpt:
2. Prompting vs Fine-Tuning vs RAG

What you will learn: Choosing the right architecture requires understanding tradeoffs: Prompting is fastest to iterate; RAG is ideal for dynamic, frequently changing knowledge and source citations; Fine-tuning is optimal for teaching consistent style, non-standard output syntax, and reducing latency.

title: Full Parameter vs Parameter-Efficient Tuning
source_excerpt:
3. Full Parameter vs Parameter-Efficient Tuning

What you will learn: Full parameter fine-tuning updates every weight tensor in the model, requiring immense GPU memory and risking catastrophic forgetting. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) freezes the base model and trains a tiny fraction (<1%) of parameters, saving memory while preserving core language skills.

title: Compute & Hardware Requirements
source_excerpt:
4. Compute & Hardware Requirements

What you will learn: Training neural networks demands high-bandwidth VRAM. Full-precision 16-bit training of a 7B model requires over 56GB VRAM for model weights, gradients, and optimizer states. Understanding memory calculations determines whether training requires multi-GPU clusters or single consumer cards.

title: The Anatomy of Loss in Transformer Training
source_excerpt:
5. The Anatomy of Loss in Transformer Training

What you will learn: Cross-entropy loss measures the difference between the model's predicted probability distribution over vocabulary tokens and the ground-truth target tokens. Optimizers like AdamW use backpropagated loss gradients to adjust weights and minimize prediction error over training epochs.

title: Collecting High-Quality Domain Data
source_excerpt:
6. Collecting High-Quality Domain Data

What you will learn: Dataset quality far outweighs quantity in instruction fine-tuning. 1,000 meticulously verified, diverse instruction-response pairs often outperform 50,000 noisy, redundant examples. Data must accurately reflect the exact distribution expected in production.

title: Instruction Tuning Formats (Alpaca, ChatML)
source_excerpt:
7. Instruction Tuning Formats (Alpaca, ChatML)

What you will learn: Standardizing dataset format is critical. Formats like Alpaca (Instruction, Input, Output) and ChatML (<|im_start|>system...<|im_end|>) use special delimiter tokens to structure multi-turn dialogues. Consistent formatting ensures the model learns correct speaker turn-taking.

title: Data Cleaning, Deduplication & Filtering
source_excerpt:
8. Data Cleaning, Deduplication & Filtering

What you will learn: Noisy data with spelling errors, factual inaccuracies, or duplicate examples degrades fine-tuned models. Applying exact and fuzzy deduplication (MinHash LSH), length filtering, and automated quality filters produces clean, high-signal training sets.

title: Synthetic Data Generation with Frontier Models
source_excerpt:
9. Synthetic Data Generation with Frontier Models

What you will learn: Frontier models can generate, expand, and critique synthetic training data using techniques like UltraFeedback and Evol-Instruct. Generating complex reasoning variations from seed questions rapidly scales high-quality training corpuses.

title: Tokenization Nuances & Padding Strategy
source_excerpt:
10. Tokenization Nuances & Padding Strategy

What you will learn: Tokenizers convert text to integer IDs. During batch training, sequences of varying lengths are padded. Applying attention masks to ignore padding tokens and packing multiple short samples into single context windows maximizes GPU compute efficiency.

title: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) Theory
source_excerpt:
11. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) Theory

What you will learn: LoRA freezes the base model weights W0 and represents weight updates ΔW as the matrix product of two low-rank matrices B and A (ΔW = B × A), where rank r is much smaller than hidden dimension d. This reduces trainable parameters by over 99%.

title: Choosing LoRA Rank (r) and Alpha (α)
source_excerpt:
12. Choosing LoRA Rank (r) and Alpha (α)

What you will learn: Rank r determines adapter capacity (typical values: 8 to 64), while alpha (α) is a scaling factor that controls adapter influence (commonly set to 2 × r). Higher rank captures more complex tasks but increases VRAM usage and risk of overfitting.

title: Target Modules (q_proj, v_proj, mlp)
source_excerpt:
13. Target Modules (q_proj, v_proj, mlp)

What you will learn: Initial LoRA implementations targeted only attention query (q_proj) and value (v_proj) matrices. Modern research demonstrates that applying LoRA to all linear layers (including key, output, and MLP up/down projections) achieves superior task adaptation with minimal extra parameters.

title: Memory Savings & Mathematical Decomposition
source_excerpt:
14. Memory Savings & Mathematical Decomposition

What you will learn: Because LoRA freezes base weights, optimizer states are only stored for the tiny low-rank matrices A and B. This drastically slashes optimizer VRAM overhead (e.g. from 16 bytes per parameter in AdamW to a fraction of a megabyte for the adapter).

title: Merging LoRA Weights into Base Models
source_excerpt:
15. Merging LoRA Weights into Base Models

What you will learn: After training, the low-rank update matrix ΔW = (α/r)(B × A) can be mathematically added directly into the frozen base weights W_new = W0 + ΔW. This merges the adapter permanently, allowing deployment with zero inference latency overhead.

title: Post-Training Quantization vs Quantized Training
source_excerpt:
16. Post-Training Quantization vs Quantized Training

What you will learn: Quantization reduces numerical precision of weights (e.g., from 16-bit float FP16 to 4-bit integer INT4). While post-training quantization simply rounds weights, quantized training backpropagates gradients through frozen low-precision weights into high-precision adapters.

title: 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) Data Type
source_excerpt:
17. 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) Data Type

What you will learn: NormalFloat (NF4) is an information-theoretically optimal quantile quantization data type designed for normally distributed neural network weights. It preserves higher precision near zero where most weights reside compared to standard uniform INT4.

title: Double Quantization & Paged Optimizers
source_excerpt:
18. Double Quantization & Paged Optimizers

What you will learn: Double Quantization quantizes the quantization constants themselves, saving ~0.37 bits per parameter. Paged Optimizers utilize CUDA Unified Memory to automatically page optimizer memory to CPU RAM during activation spikes, preventing out-of-memory crashes.

title: Training 70B Models on Consumer GPUs
source_excerpt:
19. Training 70B Models on Consumer GPUs

What you will learn: Combining NF4 quantization, Double Quantization, Paged Optimizers, and LoRA (QLoRA) enables fine-tuning massive 70-billion parameter models on a single 48GB workstation GPU or 4090 GPU without perceptible quality loss.

title: Quantization Degradation & Calibration
source_excerpt:
20. Quantization Degradation & Calibration

What you will learn: Severe quantization below 4 bits can cause perplexity degradation and outlier activation clipping. Using calibration datasets and activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) protects critical outlier weights from precision loss.

title: Learning Rate Schedules & Warmup
source_excerpt:
21. Learning Rate Schedules & Warmup

What you will learn: Learning rate is the most sensitive fine-tuning hyperparameter. Using a linear or cosine warmup for the first 5-10% of training steps stabilizes initial weight trajectory, followed by cosine decay to smoothly converge to a low-loss minimum.

title: Batch Size, Gradient Accumulation & Steps
source_excerpt:
22. Batch Size, Gradient Accumulation & Steps

What you will learn: When GPU memory limits physical batch size, gradient accumulation accumulates loss gradients across multiple forward/backward micro-steps before updating weights. This simulates large effective batch sizes without exceeding VRAM bounds.

title: Overfitting, Catastrophic Forgetting & Regularization
source_excerpt:
23. Overfitting, Catastrophic Forgetting & Regularization

What you will learn: Training for too many epochs on a narrow dataset causes the model to memorize samples and forget general reasoning abilities. Applying weight decay, dropout, early stopping, and mixing in a small percentage of general pre-training data preserves generalization.

title: Loss Curves & Evaluation Benchmarks
source_excerpt:
24. Loss Curves & Evaluation Benchmarks

What you will learn: Monitoring training vs validation loss curves identifies the optimal stopping point before validation loss diverges. Evaluating on held-out benchmark datasets at regular step intervals provides objective convergence metrics.

title: Checkpoint Management & Model Saving
source_excerpt:
25. Checkpoint Management & Model Saving

What you will learn: Training runs can crash due to hardware faults. Saving periodic checkpoints with optimizer states, loss logs, and adapter weights ensures training can resume seamlessly from the latest healthy state without loss of progress.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
source_excerpt:
26. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)

What you will learn: RLHF aligns model outputs with human preferences for helpfulness, accuracy, and safety. The classic pipeline involves training a separate reward model on human-ranked pairs and optimizing the policy model using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).

title: Reward Modeling Architecture
source_excerpt:
27. Reward Modeling Architecture

What you will learn: A reward model takes a prompt and candidate completion and outputs a scalar reward score reflecting human preference. The reward model is trained using binary cross-entropy loss on pairwise comparison datasets where humans selected preferred completions.

title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
source_excerpt:
28. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)

What you will learn: DPO eliminates the need for a separate reward model and complex reinforcement learning loops. It derives an exact closed-form loss function that directly optimizes model policy on chosen vs rejected response pairs using standard cross-entropy backpropagation.

title: Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO)
source_excerpt:
29. Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO)

What you will learn: KTO optimizes models directly on binary feedback (thumbs up / thumbs down) rather than requiring paired comparisons. Grounded in behavioral prospect theory, KTO maximizes utility directly on individual labeled examples.

title: Mitigating Sycophancy & Alignment Tax
source_excerpt:
30. Mitigating Sycophancy & Alignment Tax

What you will learn: Over-aligned models often exhibit sycophancy—agreeing with user misconceptions—or lose raw reasoning capability (the 'alignment tax'). Careful reward shaping and balance datasets ensure models remain truthful and logically rigorous.

title: Code Generation & Repository Tuning
source_excerpt:
31. Code Generation & Repository Tuning

What you will learn: Fine-tuning on code requires understanding project-level context, abstract syntax trees, and commit histories. Formatting training data with repo file paths, docstrings, and unit tests produces models capable of accurate codebase completions.

title: Medical, Legal & Financial Specialization
source_excerpt:
32. Medical, Legal & Financial Specialization

What you will learn: Regulated domains demand strict adherence to statutory terminology, citation formats, and risk disclosure. Training on specialized corpora with expert annotations ensures accurate domain jargon usage without hallucinating imaginary legal clauses.

title: Multilingual & Low-Resource Adaptation
source_excerpt:
33. Multilingual & Low-Resource Adaptation

What you will learn: Adapting models to low-resource languages involves extending tokenizer vocabularies and fine-tuning on parallel translation pairs and monolingual text to bridge semantic representations across linguistic boundaries.

title: Structured Function-Calling Specialization
source_excerpt:
34. Structured Function-Calling Specialization

What you will learn: Training models to act as deterministic API callers involves fine-tuning on thousands of multi-turn function schema definitions, parameter extraction cases, and malformed API error recovery scenarios.

title: Continual Pre-Training on Raw Text
source_excerpt:
35. Continual Pre-Training on Raw Text

What you will learn: When domain terminology is fundamentally absent from the base model, continual pre-training (causal language modeling on raw domain textbooks and papers) teaches foundational vocabulary before applying instruction tuning.

title: vLLM & High-Throughput Serving
source_excerpt:
36. vLLM & High-Throughput Serving

What you will learn: Deploying fine-tuned models in production requires high-throughput inference engines. vLLM implements PagedAttention, which manages KV cache memory like virtual memory pages in operating systems, eliminating memory fragmentation and boosting throughput 10x.

title: PagedAttention & Continuous Batching
source_excerpt:
37. PagedAttention & Continuous Batching

What you will learn: Traditional static batching waits for the slowest request in a batch to finish before accepting new queries. Continuous iteration-level batching dynamically inserts incoming requests and evicts finished requests on every single decoding step.

title: Speculative Decoding & Draft Models
source_excerpt:
38. Speculative Decoding & Draft Models

What you will learn: Speculative decoding uses a tiny, fast draft model to generate candidate token sequences which the large fine-tuned model verifies in parallel in a single forward pass, accelerating generation speed by 2x to 3x with zero loss in output quality.

title: Evaluation Suites (MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench)
source_excerpt:
39. Evaluation Suites (MMLU, HumanEval, MT-Bench)

What you will learn: Standardized benchmarks evaluate multi-task knowledge (MMLU), Python coding proficiency (HumanEval), and multi-turn conversational quality (MT-Bench). Automated evaluation suites provide objective scorecards before releasing model updates.

title: LoRA Adapter Hot-Swapping in Production
source_excerpt:
40. LoRA Adapter Hot-Swapping in Production

What you will learn: In multi-tenant environments, serving multiple full models wastes GPU memory. Multi-LoRA serving systems load a single shared frozen base model in VRAM and dynamically swap lightweight LoRA adapters on a per-request basis with microsecond latency.

title: Production Monitoring & Drift Detection
source_excerpt:
41. Production Monitoring & Drift Detection

What you will learn: Once deployed, production models require continuous monitoring of token throughput, latency percentiles (P95, P99), user feedback ratings, and semantic drift in user queries to trigger automated retraining pipelines.
